title: He Kept Winning Medals for Battles. This Cart Is What He Couldn't Stop Painting.
standfirst: Giovanni Fattori built his early reputation on Risorgimento battle scenes and the prizes that came with them. What he actually kept making, outdoors, on small wood panels, for the best part of forty years, was a farmer with a cart and a pair of oxen — and by his own working method, a panel like this one usually wasn't even meant to be the finished thing.

sections.heading: Working Sketch, Not Finished Statement
sections.body: Fattori's outdoor studies were, by his usual method, not intended to stand alone. His plein-air sketches were typically laid down on small wood panels close to this one's size, then kept as reference material for larger, more ambitious compositions built afterward in the studio — pieces like his 1887 *Branding of the Colts in the Maremma*. A panel of a farmer, a cart and two oxen, in other words, was routinely a working note rather than a statement in itself: the equivalent of a sketchbook page that happened to survive, get sold and end up on a gallery wall a century later carrying a proper title and a date.

sections.heading: The Career He Actually Wanted
sections.body: Fattori was born in Livorno on 6 September 1825, apprenticed to the painter Giuseppe Baldini, and moved to Florence the following year to study under Giuseppe Bezzuoli. In 1848 he broke off his studies to work as a courier for the anti-Austrian democratic movement. What he set out to paint, through his twenties and thirties, was history: the *Concorso Ricasoli*, a competition for a patriotic battle scene, which he won in 1859 with a prize large enough to let him marry Settimia Vannucci that July, and later *Il campo italiano dopo la battaglia di Magenta*, a large canvas of the Italian camp after the Battle of Magenta. In 1870 he took an award at the Parma exhibition for a battle scene of Prince Amedeo wounded at Custoza. That was the career he was building: prizes, patriotic subjects, a name attached to the Risorgimento's own history.

sections.heading: The Summer That Changed the Subject
sections.body: Settimia died of tuberculosis in March 1867, after Fattori had spent the previous six years largely in Livorno nursing her rather than painting battles. That summer he went to Castiglioncello to stay with the critic Diego Martelli, the Macchiaioli's chief theorist, working alongside the painter Giuseppe Abbati on landscapes and studies of rural life done straight from the motif — work he later described in terms of bold design within geometrical simplicity, and an intense luminosity. It's not possible to say the grief caused the subject; the record doesn't work that cleanly. But the sequence is exact: a history painter loses his wife, spends the following summer painting fields and farm labour instead of soldiers, and keeps doing it, in one form or another, for the rest of his life.

sections.heading: The Friend Who Tried to Import the Real Thing
sections.body: Martelli is a large part of why the corpus files this painting as Impressionism, and why that filing sits awkwardly. He had known the Macchiaioli since the mid-1850s and became their principal advocate after inheriting the Castiglioncello estate in 1861, turning it into a working retreat for Fattori's circle. But his own sympathies kept moving toward Paris: during a stay there in 1878–79 he grew close to Edgar Degas, who [painted two portraits of him that year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Martelli), and closer still to Camille Pissarro, whom he then persuaded to exhibit in Florence. The show was received badly. The Macchiaioli and the French Impressionists overlapped in time and shared a friend in Martelli, but they were never quite the same project, and the one occasion someone tried to prove otherwise in Florence, on Martelli's own recommendation, the audience didn't buy it.

sections.heading: What the Prizes Didn't Pay For
sections.body: None of the medals added up to a living. By the end of the 1870s Fattori was, by most accounts, in real poverty despite the professorship he had held at the Florence Accademia since 1869; his taxes went unpaid, his Florence property was confiscated, and a broken kneecap made things worse. From 1884 he turned hard into etching — cheaper materials than canvas — and kept the same rural subjects there too. In 1889 an etching titled *Bovi al Carro*, oxen at the cart, won him an honourable mention; at the 1900 Paris Exposition Universelle, the same subject in the same medium won him a gold medal — in the very year this panel is dated. He did not describe these years generously. "I have spent my years hoping," he wrote, "and I will end discouraged," and, on belief: "I am an atheist because I do not believe that there must be a God upon which good and evil depend."

sections.heading: What Actually Stayed
sections.body: Fattori married twice more after Settimia — Marianna Bigozzi Martinelli in 1891, and, following her death, Fanny Marinelli in 1906 — and went on teaching at the Accademia into old age. In 1902 a young Livorno painter named Amedeo Modigliani, already trained by Fattori's former pupil Guglielmo Micheli, enrolled in its life-drawing class; Fattori never taught him directly, but visited the studio and [approved of what he saw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amedeo_Modigliani) there. Fattori died in Florence on 30 August 1908. The museum that now carries his name, in Livorno's Villa Mimbelli, was built after his death on a donation of roughly 250 drawings and 150 etchings — the private, repeated, working record of exactly this kind of subject, rather than the battle scenes the medals had once been for.
